title: I quit my marketing job to walk dogs for 4 months: It's 'one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had'

body: One early morning in 2022, I found myself watching a dog walker on TikTok and thinking: I want her job.It felt ridiculous. I was finishing up my MBA and navigating the next chapter of my career with a focus on prestige and financial success. But soon after relocating from Kentucky to California in October 2021, I burned out. I had transitioned into a remote healthcare marketing role, living on the West Coast but still working East Coast hours and completing my second year of business school from afar. While everyone around me seemed to be heading to the beach and enjoying the sunshine, I spent my days inside, glued to a computer screen.The dog walker I followed online seemed to have everything I was craving: fresh air, movement, flexibility and a job that didn't revolve around emails and Zoom meetings.During a long drive, I joked with my husband, "I think I'm going to quit my job and walk dogs." The joke quickly became a plan.My season as a professional dog walkerWithin the span of just a few weeks in the spring of 2022, I quit my job, graduated from business school, traveled to Europe for an old roommate's wedding and then flew to Texas to speak at the Latino Franchise Symposium. While I was there, I created my Rover profile. I highlighted my experience volunteering at animal shelters in college, pet sitting for friends and caring for animals throughout my life.Before I even made it back home to California, I had my first meet-and-greet scheduled with a potential client. Shortly after, I landed my first booking. I was thrilled.At first, I intentionally priced my services below what seemed typical in my area to build reviews, charging about $15 for a drop-in visit and about $17 for a 30-minute walk. Some days I had just one client. I was able to start small because I had savings to tide me over, along with a partner whose job provided steady income and benefits.My goal was to become the person people trusted with a member of their family.Courtesy of Sally SimmonsStill, I treated it like a real business from day one. I accepted nearly every opportunity that came my way, taking dogs on midday walks, housesitting on weekends and boarding dogs in my apartment.I sent thoughtful updates to the dog owners filled with photos, detailed notes and plenty of emojis. I shared bathroom break tallies, funny moments and anything unusual they should know. If I stayed overnight, I brought in packages, cleaned up after myself and made sure their home looked exactly as they had left it.My goal wasn't simply to complete the booking. It was to become the person people trusted with a member of their family.The reviews started rolling in. As my profile gained traction, I gradually increased my rates, eventually charging $23 for a drop-in visit and $84 for overnight stays. By the time I left the platform four months later, I had earned a five-star rating with 30 reviews, built a roster of recurring clients and filled my calendar.Walking dogs gave me space to think and reflect on what success actually meant, what I wanted my career to look like and, perhaps more importantly, how I wanted my days to feel.Christina Locopo | CNBC Make It; Courtesy of Sally SimmonsOne of my favorite memories came when a family asked me to care for their dogs during their wedding weekend. I spent two and a half days at a beautiful resort and dressed the dogs in tiny tuxedos before they walked down the aisle.It reminded me that this work was about helping families enjoy some of the biggest moments of their lives with peace of mind. Years later, we're still friends. They now have a daughter, and my daughter and I recently attended her first birthday party.A new definition of successSome days I walked more than eight miles, logging over 18,000 steps as I explored neighborhoods I otherwise never would have discovered. I spent hours outside instead of sitting behind a desk. Sometimes I listened to podcasts or music. Other times, I simply enjoyed the quiet.Those walks gave me space to think. I reflected on what success actually meant, what I wanted my career to look like and, perhaps more importantly, how I wanted my days to feel.Before Rover, success meant getting promotions, landing bigger clients and climbing the corporate ladder. Walking dogs challenged that definition. I realized I didn't want to chase an impressive title as much as I wanted to chase a lifestyle that gave me energy.Ironically, it was during one of those walks that I received the phone call offering me the marketing job I still have today. I paused on the sidewalk, accepted the offer and then finished the walk.I put a photo of me and my husband holding our own pets (left) on my Rover profile. Long after my dog-walking era, I stayed friends with the dogs Tofu and Noodles (right) and their humans.Courtesy of Sally SimmonsReturning to marketing wasn't a difficult decision. By then, I was pregnant with my first daughter and needed the stability, benefits and predictable income that came with a full-time role. When an excited dog chasing a squirrel pulled me to the ground early in my pregnancy, it became clear that my season as a professional dog walker was coming to an end.Still, I think about those four months often. People sometimes assume dog walking was a gap or detour in my career. I see it as one of the most valuable professional experiences I've ever had.It reminded me that passion is visible, no matter what kind of work you're doing. It reinforced that the skills that matter most — showing up, listening, caring deeply, building trust and making small, consistent changes — translate to every career.And even though I'm back in marketing, my days look different than they did before my dog-walking era. These days, you'll find me logging off at 5 p.m. to go play outside with my family before dinner, walking near the ocean after a hard week, having kitchen dance parties to shake off the day, taking calls while walking my own dog or squeezing in a lunchtime workout. The fresh air and sense of presence give me the balance I craved when I was glued to screens on a schedule dictated by someone else's time zone.Those four months taught me something my MBA never could: Success isn't just about finding a job that sounds impressive. It's about building a life you genuinely enjoy living, even if it doesn't look like the one you originally imagined.Sally Simmons is a marketing leader and holistic health coach based in California. After years building strategies for global brands, she found unexpected lessons about business, connection and success during a four-month chapter as a professional dog walker. Today, she brings those lessons into her work helping people create healthier, more balanced lives.

title: Audi defends plans for a $4 billion Georgia plant amid VW restructuring, tariffs
description: The Audi logo can be seen on a car dealership in Manhattan. Picture Alliance | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesDETROIT — Audi's CEO defended the carmak
body: The Audi logo can be seen on a car dealership in Manhattan. Picture Alliance | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesDETROIT — Audi's CEO defended the carmaker's plans for a new $4 billion plant in Georgia on Sunday, calling it a business decision aimed at growing sales and reducing exposure to U.S. tariffs.The plant, set to be Audi's first in the U.S., was announced Saturday by President Donald Trump during a rally in Georgia, near where the Volkswagen-owned luxury brand plans to build the new SUV-producing facility."We have significantly greater ambitions for Audi in America," Audi CEO Gernot Dollner said during a media roundtable Sunday. "The United States is the second largest premium market in the world, and today we are not fully exploiting this potential. We are changing that."The announcement comes amid an intense restructuring of its VW parent company, including plans to cut 50,000 jobs and close four German plants, including an Audi facility, between 2031 and ​2034.Dollner, who joined Trump at the rally, said the decision for a plant in the U.S. was years in the making, with more than 70 locations evaluated over "many months" and "intense" negotiations with public officials."This is not a decision against Germany. Germany remains the backbone of Audi," Dollner said. "We develop our cars here. Our technologies are created here, and Georgia does not take any task away from us in Germany."watch nowDollner said localized production is the best decision for the brand, which has struggled in sales this decade amid rising operational costs and Trump's tariffs on vehicles from Germany and other countries into the U.S. Current tariffs on vehicles from Germany are 15%, down from 25%.Last year, U.S. tariffs cost Audi 1.2 billion euros ($1.4 billion), as it imports all its vehicles for the U.S. market from Europe or Mexico.Dollner said the Trump administration asked Audi to announce the new plant at the Georgia rally promoting Republicans ahead of Nov. 3 midterm elections."It was … a three-year project that, at the end, by coincidence, led to that moment yesterday," he said Sunday. "With respect of the office and country, we joined the invitation."Dollner noted Audi is the last major German luxury brand to establish U.S. production after Mercedes-Benz and BMW.The company said the Georgia plant is expected to begin production of Audi's Q7, Q8 and Q9 in the early 2030s. The plant would have the capacity to produce up to 200,000 vehicles annually, roughly half of which the automaker said will be exported outside the U.S."This is to make Audi obviously a significant player here in the U.S. market," said Audi of America President Vito Paladino during the roundtable. He also said additional details on U.S. investments and production are forthcoming.Audi's U.S. deliveries were roughly flat through the third quarter of this year, following a 16% decline from 2024 to 2025.

schema.headline: Audi defends plans for a $4 billion Georgia plant amid VW restructuring, tariffs

title: American embassies tighten security as Iran threat warnings intensify ahead of U.S. midterm elections
description: The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.AFP via Getty ImagesU.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East
body: The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.AFP via Getty ImagesU.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday.A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report, and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well. The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu. Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June. Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal. Later in the day, Iranian state media denied the report.The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month.Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high. U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.8% to settle over $103 a barrel. watch now

title: Blanche defends Trump-ordered lawsuit over Alaska Senate election certification
description: Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche (C) leaves after a meeting with Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) and Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) at the U.S. Capitol
body: Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche (C) leaves after a meeting with Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) and Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) at the U.S. Capitol on Aug. 5, 2026 in Washington, DC. Alex Wong | Getty ImagesAttorney General Todd Blanche defended the Justice Department's lawsuit on Sunday seeking to block certification of Alaska's Senate election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowly loses. The lawsuit, filed last week, cites what it argues is likely voter confusion over the name Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher also on the ballot. The DOJ said confusion over the two Sullivans could help former Alaska Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, who is narrowly ahead in polls just over a week from Election Day, win the election. "What we're asking the court to do is make sure that after the election, if it's clear that there was confusion, if it's clear, and that's for a court to decide at a later date if there's litigation ... and that confusion led to an unjust, improper result that is not the will of the Alaskan voter, we want to make sure that the Alaskan system and the Alaskan state courts and the Alaskan electoral process can understand that in a way that lets them do the right thing," Blanche said on CNN's "State of the Union." "Never before have opponents gone to such lengths to try and thwart and cheat in an election as they're doing in this case," he said. The DOJ's lawsuit says that the potential for voter confusion exists and Alaska should not certify the election if "(1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska's rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election."Alaska applies a top-four primary system to select candidates for the general election. The November general election uses ranked-choice voting.Ranked-choice voting lets voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of votes in the first round of counting, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated. Voters who ranked the eliminated candidate first then have their second choice counted and added to that candidate's total. This continues until a majority winner — or the candidate with more than half of the vote — wins.This combo shows U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, left, in Palmer, Alaska, on Aug. 17, 2026 and a candidate in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, Dan J. Sullivan, right, in Petersburg, Alaska, on July 3, 2026.AP Photos | Mark Thiessen | Becky BohrerRepublicans have argued for months that Daniel J. Sullivan is a Democratic plant intended to confuse voters and have sought to remove him from the ballot. Democrats have maintained they have no connection to the candidate, and Sullivan himself has denied running to confuse voters.The Alaska Division of Elections briefly removed Daniel J. Sullivan in June, before a state court ordered his name returned to the ballot. The state Supreme Court upheld that decision.President Donald Trump, who has long made claims of voter fraud without evidence, said he ordered the DOJ's lawsuit himself. Democratic groups and voting rights advocates, including Peltola's campaign, are seeking to join the lawsuit to stop the DOJ's effort to block certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan loses. The groups argue the executive branch lacks the legal authority to intervene in state-run elections and is attempting an unprecedented override of state election administration, with early voting already underway."In an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections, the Department of Justice—acting on the President's personal orders—demands that this Court enjoin the certification of the ongoing U.S. Senate election, but only if the President's preferred candidate loses," the motion to intervene reads. "But the federal government has no power to impose that Hobson's choice on the people of this State."Rep. Mary Peltola, Alaska, poses for a picture in her Cannon Building office on Thursday, February 9, 2023.Tom Williams | Cq-roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesAlaska is seen as one of the best chances for a Democratic flip in the Nov. 3 elections, which will determine control of Congress for the remainder of Trump's term. Trump has been barnstorming competitive states in recent weeks as the polls favor Democrats to win control of the House of Representatives and potentially flip the Senate. Democrats and voting rights advocates have long feared that Trump — who denied his election loss to former President Joe Biden in 2020, leading to a violent riot at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 — would attempt to meddle in the midterm contest to save narrow Republican majorities in Congress. Blanche bristled on Sunday when asked whether the lawsuit aimed to sway the election in Alaska toward Republicans. "That is crazy," Blanche said, pressed on CNN about whether the president is laying the groundwork for a "doomsday" scenario in which he tries to overturn election results. "We're not laying any groundwork for the president to do that ... the groundwork that we are laying is for the state of Alaska, if it becomes an issue after the election, will have the ability to determine whether there was confusion that violates the law in determining who the senator should be."

schema.headline: Blanche defends Trump-ordered lawsuit over Alaska Senate election certification

title: Ukraine disputes Elon Musk’s claim that its military violated Starlink terms during drone operations
description: Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat positio
body: Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat position in the Donetsk region, Ukraine, on Oct. 16, 2026.Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesA Ukrainian official disputed SpaceX CEO Elon Musk's claim that Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service, prompting the company to restrict Ukraine's access to the high-speed satellite technology.Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote an online post on Sunday contesting Musk's reason for temporarily throttling Ukraine's access to high-speed service from SpaceX's Starlink satellite communication systems. Ukrainian officials previously said the restrictions disrupted the country's military drone services and left the country vulnerable to Russian attacks.Musk on Saturday claimed in a post on X that the "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people."Beskrestnov pushed back on Musk's allegation, arguing that pre-existing restrictions on the systems would have made it "physically impossible" for Ukraine to use Starlink in the types of strikes the SpaceX CEO described."It is very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine," Beskrestnov wrote in a post on Telegram, noting that Starlink's civilian system in Ukraine "does not function over the territory of Russia" and that Ukrainian drones operating with Starlink have had a speed restriction of 70 to 90 km/h (roughly 43 to 56 miles per hour) for months."Consequently, it is PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE for us to use commercial Starlink for deep-strike or medium-range strike operations," Beskrestnov wrote.Ukraine officials acknowledged on Saturday that high-speed service for SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield satellite communications systems had been restored. The country has blamed that restricted service for disrupting its drone air defense capabilities during frequent Russian air attacks.Starshield is SpaceX's military-focused satellite network for government and national security use, built on technology developed for Starlink, the company's broader commercial satellite internet network.Before Musk acknowledged that he had restricted the systems, confusion and speculation abounded over who ordered the high-speed service changes.At one point, Musk wrote in a social media post that the U.S. government was behind the decision, though President Donald Trump claimed he had no knowledge of the decision. Ukrainian officials have also said Starlink or the U.S. had imposed the restrictions without warning, leaving the country blindsided. Musk has not explained the reported lack of notification to Ukraine before his company implemented the restrictions.Musk and SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment.The restrictions on Starlink and Starshield in war-torn Ukraine have driven Ukraine and its allies to seek or build alternative, "sovereign" satellite communication systems. Poland's Deputy Minister of National Defense, Cezary Tomczyk, discussed his country's plans on a podcast called Influence Zone (Strefa Influenceów) earlier this month. Ukraine also announced partnerships with Norway and Finland's mobile giant Nokia, as well as satellite maker ICEYE, to develop alternatives.Beyond Ukraine, several countries are also exploring sovereign systems. The European Union is building IRIS², a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but it doesn't expect its first launches until 2029.SpaceX's Starlink generated $5.25 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up from $3.1 billion a year earlier. Revenue from consumer Starlink subscribers totaled $3.12 billion, while the company generated $2.13 billion from government and enterprise customers during the quarter.A wide array of customers, including non-government entities, the governments of Poland and France, and the Pentagon, have paid SpaceX to provide its Starlink and Starshield hardware and wireless internet services to Ukraine.

title: What Democrats and Republicans fear most about each other: CNBC survey has the answers
description: watch nowIf Democrats take over Congress, Republican voters are worried they'll move too far to the left and enact socialist policies. If Republicans
body: watch nowIf Democrats take over Congress, Republican voters are worried they'll move too far to the left and enact socialist policies. If Republicans keep control, Democrats fret about President Donald Trump having unchecked power.Those are the findings from a new CNBC poll that shows what each side of the political divide fears about the other as the midterm election looms. Republicans in the survey also say they worry about weakened border security and higher taxes under a Democratic Congress. Democrats say they're concerned about continued Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportations and ongoing military efforts in Iran under a Republican one."That totally shows the polarization … and the fear that one side is going to completely undo the agenda of the other," Ron Bonjean, a Republican strategist and co-founder of ROKK Solutions, said of the results. "What Republicans are worried about is that Democrats are going to go back to the way it was during the Biden administration."The results of the latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey — conducted between Oct. 14 and 18 and including 1,000 registered voters — could serve as a warning for both parties after the election. Both Democrats and Republicans have struggled with low favorability amid widespread distrust of the government.If Democrats lurch too far to the left and adopt Democratic Socialists of America policies, they could squander the gains some forecasts project they could make in many heavily Republican parts of the country, said Lucas Holtz, a senior political advisor at Third Way, a center-left think tank. "They should not misread their mandate if they hope to retain the inroads that they're making this cycle with Latino voters, with working-class voters, who they have been hemorrhaging cycle after cycle," Holtz said. And Republicans should understand that voters in this moment want to change course, Bonjean said."Voters absolutely want change from the way things are going now, but they also don't want to go back to the way things were when Democrats ran Washington," Bonjean said. "The branding is so bad on the Democratic side, and it's not great on the Republican side."Respondents were able to select up to two of their biggest concerns in the event that Democrats or Republicans control Congress, which don't necessarily indicate their top electoral priorities. The CNBC survey by Hart Research Associates and Public Opinion Strategies separately asked people to name the most important issues facing the country. In answering that question, affordability issues ranked highly across the political spectrum, while Democrats and independents also listed government corruption as a top priority, and Republicans listed immigration and border security.Still, the concerns expressed by voters about what the opposing party might do in office reflect the messages in the political advertising that is blanketing much of the country in the final days before the midterm election, according to Alex Jacquez, senior vice president of policy, advocacy, and research at Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive think tank. Democrats on the campaign trail have hammered Trump for his alleged corruption and Republicans have attempted to paint Democrats as overly progressive."For Democrats, the main attack ads [targeting them] have ... been about DSA and they've been about the cultural issues that Republicans are trying to hit to tie them to a kind of a far-left or radical movement," Jacquez said. "But the overall vibe of the election is still first and foremost about the economy, people tend to blame the president for prices and Congress for enabling him."If Democrats gain control of Congress, 22% of all voters said they are concerned about them failing to bring down prices, including 31% of Democrats, 22% of independents and 15% of Republicans. In the event the GOP retains the gavels in the House and Senate, 24% of voters said they worry whether prices will come down, including 32% of Republicans, 22% of independents and 17% of Democrats.But those worries trail fears about checking Trump and policies associated with the DSA, a political organization that has notched recent wins in places like New York City, Washington and Denver and advocates progressive social and populist economic policies.Of all voters polled, 44% said they fear Trump would be allowed to operate beyond his constitutional power, including 74% of Democrats and 45% of independents. Twenty-eight percent of respondents said they are concerned with the implementation of DSA policies, including 54% of Republicans and 22% of independents.

schema.headline: What Democrats and Republicans fear most about each other: CNBC survey has the answers

title: Trump is pushing a massive AI buildout. His own voters are wary of what comes with it
description: watch nowPresident Donald Trump has cast America's artificial intelligence race with China as a national-security imperative, pushing faster developme
body: watch nowPresident Donald Trump has cast America's artificial intelligence race with China as a national-security imperative, pushing faster development of the technology and an immense buildout of the data centers and power infrastructure needed to fuel it.But the new CNBC All-America Economic Survey reveals a growing political tension beneath that agenda: Republican voters broadly support the push for AI development, but many oppose building the sprawling infrastructure needed to power it in their own backyards.Nearly 55% of MAGA supporters want companies to keep developing advanced AI while Congress works on regulations, versus 27% who favor a pause. But only 29% would support a data center within 10 miles of their home, while 40% oppose one. Among all Republicans and Republican-leaning voters — not just those who identify themselves with the MAGA movement — those who say they would support a data center near their home falls to 24%.  Across the electorate, 63% don't want a nearby AI data center and just 13% support one. Democrats lead the opposition: 80% oppose nearby facilities while just 4% support them. That resistance is increasingly forcing Trump and vulnerable Republicans who once championed data centers to recalibrate as they head into a bleak midterm election environment for the party."Many people are annoyed by these data centers," said Brad Carson, a former Democratic congressman from Oklahoma and co-founder of Public First Action PAC, an AI-industry-backed political group pushing for stronger regulation and safeguards. "People are also strongly insistent upon reasonable guardrails of AI, and that's going to be hard to beat."The CNBC survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide was conducted Oct. 14-18 by Hart Research Associates and Public Opinion Strategies and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. The data-center proximity question was asked of a half-sample of roughly 500 voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.38 percentage points.Read the full survey results here.The politics have shifted from the early AI boom, when Washington and Silicon Valley sold the technology as an avenue for investment, growth and American dominance.But as the buildout accelerates, its physical costs are becoming harder to ignore. Communities are fighting data centers over spiking electric bills, soaring electricity and water demand, noise, land use and taxpayer subsidies. Coupled with job-displacement fears from AI, opponents now point to the facilities as a physical symbol of who benefits from the boom and who gets stuck with the bill.The industry rejects that framing. “The data center industry provides significant, tangible benefits,” said Dan Diorio of the Data Center Coalition, pointing to jobs, investment and tax revenue while adding that operators are committed to “paying for the energy we use."But when asked their top concerns if Republicans retain Congress, 18% of voters in the survey cited a failure to regulate AI and data centers. That tied continued military efforts in Iran and outranked continued Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportations at 15%, cuts to health insurance subsidies at 10% and an extension of Trump's tariffs at 5%.Even among voters who want Republicans to retain control, 17% cited weak AI and data center oversight — second only to a failure to bring down prices.GOP strategists have taken note.  In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned AI companies that data center backlash was threatening Sen. Jon Husted's reelection in Ohio, calling the issue a midterm "sleeper" that could sour politicians nationwide on future projects, Axios reported.As Ohio lieutenant governor in 2024, Husted helped announce a $10 billion Amazon Web Services expansion, calling AI facilities "crucial to America's economic superiority." Now, in a tight Senate race against Democrat Sherrod Brown, who has made data-center opposition a campaign issue, Husted is promoting stalled legislation to make large facilities cover their own grid and generation costs rather than pass them on to residential ratepayers.Texas tells a similar story. Less than a year after Gov. Greg Abbott hailed the state as an "epicenter of AI development," he halted data center permits pending grid- and water-impact reviews and called for ending state tax incentives.Trump himself is showing signs of the political pressure. In a Truth Social post Wednesday, he said data center developers should pay host communities a financial "dividend" and generate their own power, arguing that local payouts can turn unpopular projects into popular ones.For now, Democrats hold a modest edge on managing the issue: 32% of voters trust them to handle data center expansion, versus 24% for the Republicans. But 27% said neither party would do a better job than the other.And the CNBC survey indicates this skepticism runs deeper than local zoning. Overall, 52% of registered voters want advanced AI development paused until Congress passes safety regulations, compared to 32% who favor moving ahead to keep pace with China. Democrats remain far more cautious: 70% favor a pause, while just 18% support pushing forward. "The debate has shifted dramatically," Carson told CNBC. "A year ago, there were many people who said, 'Let it cook, no regulation at all, exempt the companies from normal rules.'" Carson said sentiment toward AI has "deteriorated a lot over the last six months."

title: Turmoil hits AI buildout as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO
description: CoreWeave founder and CEO Mike Intrator poses for a photo during the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq headquarters in New York, March 2
body: CoreWeave founder and CEO Mike Intrator poses for a photo during the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq headquarters in New York, March 28, 2025.Michael M. Santiago | Getty ImagesNeoclouds tanked. Credit default swaps soared. Meta turned cash flow negative. And SK Hynix's Solidigm unit canceled plans for its initial public offering.It's been a rocky week for the AI infrastructure trade. The Nasdaq followed Thursday's beating with an additional drop on Friday to end the week down 0.7%. Among the hyperscalers, the worst performer was Alphabet, shares of which sank 6% ahead of the internet giant's third-quarter earnings report next week. Microsoft and Amazon are also on the docket, and they each saw shares fall less than 1%.While the tech market has thus far avoided a dramatic across-the-board sell-off, the artificial intelligence buildout is showing signs of strain. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN all fell sharply this week, bringing their losses for October to well over 30% each. CoreWeave, the leader of the pack, has seen spreads on its CDS widen past 11%, generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default. Meanwhile, yields on the company's 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes topped 15%. "What investors are doing is throwing every baby out with the bathwater and saying anyone who is a neocloud" will be devalued, Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday.watch nowFears aren't limited to the U.S. market. Shares of Elice Group, a South Korean cloud provider, dropped 30% in their market debut on Tuesday, and shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast. AI optimism has been the major market driver for the past couple of years, as unrelenting demand for new models and services pushes the world's biggest tech companies to spend on infrastructure at historic rates. However, skeptics are getting more vocal in their concerns that returns on AI investment won't justify the capital expenditures.Analysts at research and advisory firm Gartner predict that 80% of neocloud companies will either cease operations or be absorbed by 2030.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, perhaps the leading AI evangelist, remains bullish. Huang said this week at a company conference in Berlin that "demand for the neoclouds is off the charts.""The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal. "That's going to get solved."Withdrawn IPOWall Street isn't convinced. On Thursday, South Korean memory giant SK Hynix, one of the biggest winners in the AI boom, said it's pulling an IPO for its U.S.-based Solidigm unit, citing market volatility. SK Hynix purchased Solidigm, which makes NAND and SSD storage for data centers, from Intel in 2021."While an IPO was expected to ease investment burdens and expand capacity for shareholder returns, the review has been discontinued in light of market conditions and share price trends," SK Hynix said in a release. Despite the turmoil, all of tech's mega-caps have maintained their investment-grade rating even as they've opened their wallets to fuel their build-outs, including through debt. Even with that group of companies, the market is showing some jitters.Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026.Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesMeta saw its stock plunge 7% on Thursday after the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter of over $2 billion while raising the floor of its full-year capex to $135 billion from $130 billion. Meta also said it plans to spend about $825 billion over the coming years on various leases and contracts, with over $450 billion of those leases being non-cancellable take-or-pay agreements. Spreads on Meta's five-year CDS reached all-time highs of over 124 basis points. CDS on Nvidia and Oracle also touched records, with their spreads hitting 126 basis points and 343 basis points, respectively, this week. Oracle's stock has lost over one-third of its value this year, and now the company faces risks of a credit rating downgrade.John Williams, who leads the derivatives practice at law firm Milbank LLP, says investors are seeking numerous ways beyond buying CDS to hedge their bets with respect to the AI trade.  "There's so much investment going into it that it's just very appropriate to look for risk management tools, completely regardless of whether you're bullish or bearish," Williams said. "It would be crazy for people not to be looking for appropriate risk management tools for it."Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, told CNBC's "SquawkBox Asia" last week that it's "all kind of tied together," referring to AI's impact on the whole market. "Can you drop a bowling ball in one part of the pool and not get any waves downstream to the rest of the Nasdaq?" he said. "I don't know. I have some concern about that."— CNBC's Katie Tarasov contributed to this reportWATCH: Concerned about rising CDS spreads in data center build-outwatch now

title: Corruption is voters' top issue ahead of midterm election, CNBC survey shows
description: watch nowVoters are now more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices, according to the final
body: watch nowVoters are now more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices, according to the final CNBC All-America Economic Survey before the Nov. 3 midterm election.The finding follows a monthslong messaging effort by Democrats to link widespread economic dissatisfaction with what they allege is rampant corruption by President Donald Trump and his Republican allies.CNBC's survey of 1,000 registered U.S. voters found 36% of respondents pointing to government corruption as one of the most important issues facing the country right now. The cost of food and groceries came second with 34%, followed by protecting democracy and the price of gas, which garnered 23% each.The nationwide poll, which gauged attitudes about the economy, Trump, Congress, artificial intelligence, the Iran war and more, was conducted Oct. 14-18. It was co-led by Democratic pollster Hart Research Associates and Republican pollster Public Opinion Strategies, and carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.Read the full survey results here.To be sure, the question asking voters to name their top concerns lists several economy- and cost-related topics separately, subdividing an issue that might otherwise rank higher if lumped into a single category.But the results nevertheless align with other recent polls showing corruption has shot to the top of voters' list of pressing worries.A Fox News poll published last week found 60% of registered voters are extremely concerned about government corruption, surpassing concerns about inflation and high prices. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released Sunday found some two-thirds of respondents think Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, up 10 percentage points since September 2025. Gallup recently found perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. have hit multi-decade highs. And an August poll from Reuters/Ipsos found nearly 7 in 10 Americans believe Trump's businesses influence his presidential decisions.Republicans have also tried to seize on growing anti-corruption sentiment. The Trump administration has launched a task force led by Vice President JD Vance aimed at cracking down on fraud, while the president frequently accuses his Democratic enemies of crookery."I just want to say that from day one of my administration, we've waged an unprecedented war on corruption and fraud, and will not let our country be looted and plundered by thieves and pirates and foreign fraudsters and basically scum," Trump said Tuesday while unveiling a new reward program for whistleblowers.But with Republicans in charge of the federal government — and as high costs linked to Trump's tariffs and the Iran war have put the GOP on defense — Democrats have been able to cast blame more directly."Americans have spent well over $100 BILLION extra on gas because Trump chose to go to war with Iran," Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said Wednesday on X. "His ego-fueled decisions cost you thousands."Flood lights illuminate the low rain clouds around the U.S. Capitol Building at night on October 11, 2026, in Washington, DC. J. David Ake | Getty ImagesTheir arguments often spotlight Trump, attempting to draw a contrast between Americans' widely felt financial struggles with the president's surging net worth, his family's lucrative business dealings and his focus on pricey construction projects.Other Democratic candidates have widened the scope of the message, delivering a pitch that the system itself is broken."The problem is that the people's elected representatives don't represent the people. They represent the donors and special interests," Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said in an April campaign video. "Corruption is why things don't work for ordinary people."House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has hammered the claim that Republicans have betrayed their vow to bring down costs."The wealthy and well-connected are cashing in. What are Republicans doing to lower costs for everyone else? Absolutely nothing," Jeffries wrote Friday.Rhetoric and resultsDemocrats' push appears to be resonating with voters, even as large swaths remain skeptical of both parties. Respondents to the CNBC survey gave Democrats a 4-point edge over Republicans, 35% to 31%, when asked which party would do a better job dealing with government corruption. But that gap grew to 17 points in Democrats' favor among voters who said corruption was their most important issue. And independents, by a 15-point margin, said Democrats would address corruption better than Republicans – though 41% of those respondents think neither party would do a good job.The apparent rise in concern about corruption is welcome news to critics of the president who have long lamented that Americans have become numb to scandal in the Trump era.That shift is taking place because voters are feeling the impact of inflation and connecting it to what they see in Washington, said Brian Lemek, executive of the Democrat-backing political action committee Defend the Vote, in an interview."It's the only thing people are talking about right now," said Lemek, whose group briefed candidates on the issue in June.Voters are "looking at the reality that their costs are high" and "making the connection between this corrupt and broken system and their high costs," he said.Additionally, survey respondents overwhelmingly opposed the idea of elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, personally owning or trading stocks in individual companies that have contracts with the federal government. That should not be allowed, 93% of voters said in the poll.A similar proportion – 89% – said that companies owned, or invested in, by a sitting president's immediate family members should not be allowed to receive contracts from the federal government."This definitely ties back to the corruption issues that we've been talking about," said Alicia Simmons of Hart Research Associates.

title: Why popular airplanes are getting scrapped years early
description: watch nowGOODYEAR, Ariz. — An Airbus A320neo, one of the world's most popular planes, rolled off the Mobile, Alabama, factory line in July 2022, paint
body: watch nowGOODYEAR, Ariz. — An Airbus A320neo, one of the world's most popular planes, rolled off the Mobile, Alabama, factory line in July 2022, painted bright yellow for its next destination: Spirit Airlines. It was built to fly for decades. But this May, less than four years later, it was stripped for parts worth millions and crushed, the steel teeth of an excavator tearing through its fuselage at a facility on the outskirts of Phoenix. More aircraft are getting dismantled years, if not decades, earlier than expected, industry executives told CNBC. It is the result of a shortage of parts, none more precious and expensive than aircraft engines, that has exasperated airlines and driven up costs for years.Even after the engines are removed, firms are looking for parts as varied as landing gear and antennae to sell."It's the first time in my career that involved purchasing an aircraft that's less than five years since date of manufacture," said Bill Thompson, vice president who leads aircraft and engine acquisition for the Americas at aviation asset management and trading firm EirTrade Aviation, which bought the less than 4-year-old Airbus A320neo earlier this year. An Airbus plane painted in Spirit Airlines' livery sits at an AerSale's facility in Goodyear, Arizona.Leslie Josephs / CNBCHe said the company paid "single-digit" millions each for that airplane and a similarly aged one, and it expects to make a profit from selling the more than 1,000 parts it took off them before they were crushed. "I don't know if you're going to sell the coffee makers but you never know. Sometimes you do," he said.'Don't fall in love with the metal'Twenty-one newest-generation aircraft were torn down from June 2025 through this past August, according to aviation data and advisory firm IBA Group. The scrapped planes were 6.4 years old on average, and included mostly Airbus but also some Boeing planes. That compares with an average retirement age for narrow-body airplanes of 21.7 years, IBA said."Anytime that you end up with any period of market softness in aircraft availability, engine availability, it's going to cause investors to look at other options," said Simon Goodson, CEO of AerFin, a company that buys, sells, repairs and leases aircraft and parts. "We always say to our aircraft and engine traders, 'Please don't fall in love with the metal.'"A scrapped Singapore Airlines jet at AerSale in Goodyear, Arizona.Leslie Josephs / CNBCHundreds of aircraft are retired each year as manufacturers ramp up production for airlines, so older planes are swapped out for newer, more fuel-efficient models.But aside from retiring aging planes, some owners don't want to wait around for replacement parts or repairs on younger jets. "A year might not sound that long, but does three or four years?" said Dave Querio, CEO of Ascent Aviation Services, a company that repairs, modifies, stores and disassembles aircraft, based in Marana, Arizona, outside of Tucson. "That's the issue for the aircraft that came in in '23, '24 and '25."In some cases, owners can reap more for the parts than they can selling the plane or paying storage costs and waiting for it to get back in the air again.Querio said he hasn't seen "the volume of younger aircraft being torn down as I'm seeing today."Hot engine marketA major reason for the young retirements is the long wait and rising prices for jet engines.One problem is that cutting-edge engines that burn hotter and use less fuel are coming up for maintenance far earlier than airlines expected. The maintenance requests have kept engine repair and overhaul facilities backed up, from those owned by manufacturing giants GE Aerospace and RTX unit Pratt & Whitney to smaller, independent ones. Airlines and leasing firms have been hunting for spare parts and engines anywhere they can find them, like here in Goodyear, Arizona.A Pratt & Whitney engine mounted on Spirit Airlines Airbus plane.Leslie Josephs / CNBCThe trend has added more fuel to the already hot secondhand parts market. An engine fan blade could cost $50,000 or even more than $100,000 for bigger jets, Goodson said. Engines that power some Airbus A320neo aircraft have 20 of those blades. A disc for the engine, meanwhile, could cost between $1 million and $2 million.An engine recall because of a manufacturing defect has backed up repair shops and grounded hundreds of Airbus planes around the world. Spirit Airlines bore the brunt of that problem in the United States, years before the airline collapsed.The engine is made by Pratt & Whitney, which issued the recall in 2023 after discovering contaminated powdered metal used in making some parts. Those engines are worth close to $17 million this year at the high end, up 60% from the upper end of the range in 2019, according to IBA. Airlines are removing some engines off retired planes to keep current aircraft flying while they wait for engines to come back from the shop."So you're just playing Legos and moving engines on and off aircraft," said Mike Stengel, a partner at AeroDynamic Advisory, an aerospace consulting firm.The problems are driving up the cost to buy or rent one of the popular engines to record levels.Renting one is ranging from about $160,000 to $180,000 a month, according to IBA data. A competing engine for the A320neo family made by CFM International, a joint venture of GE Aerospace and France's Safran, is far from a bargain, renting in a similar range of $130,000 to $180,000 a month.Spirit Airlines' ghost planesThe problems with young retirements predate Spirit's collapse. The 4-year-old Airbus plane that was torn down outside Phoenix in May is a key example. The aircraft was put in storage because of the engine recall, and it stayed until it was torn apart.But the company's demise has brought more of its Airbus fleet to the market, forcing owners to figure out if it's worth the wait for engines or other parts.A former Spirit Airlines airplane in storage in Goodyear, Arizona.Leslie Josephs / CNBCCNBC visited AerSale's facility in Goodyear on a scorching day in late June, less than two months after Spirit collapsed, where dozens of the idle yellow planes were stored. It was so soon after the airline's demise that a former Detroit-based Spirit captain, Glenn Zecchin, popped in and asked about opportunities to ferry Spirit's aircraft to the desert, and to peek in on his former airline's planes."I knew the airplanes were there, and I wanted to see what happened," said Zecchin, who is now flying corporate jets.A jet parked at the storage facility and maintenance hangar still had Spirit in-flight menus and safety cards in the bungee cord seatbacks. Pilot manuals were still in the cockpit.Not all of these aircraft will be destroyed. Some companies that owned Spirit's planes before bankruptcy will just sell their parts, but some may keep the planes in storage. Other aircraft may go on to fly for other airlines, with potential carriers ripping out Spirit's tight 28-inch seat pitch for something roomier.But as long as they're not flying, it means paying storage fees, which vary by aircraft type. Some planes in desert facilities — selected because the arid climate can preserve the aircraft better and avoid corrosion — can sit for decades.Others won't make it back into the air if there's enough demand for the parts and too long of a wait to get the plane flying again."After you get rid of all the valuable equipment and sell it back into the aftermarket, what's really left is just a metal carcass that you will literally take a crane and crush," said AeroDynamic's Stengel. Then the owner can "sell it to recyclers that will make of it what they will, maybe into beer cans or something outside of aerospace."Ascent's Querio said some owners opt to take that route."It's a little melancholy to watch it at times," he said. "But sometimes, it's kind of a thrill to ... see how fast an aircraft can be crunched up and sent off to the smelter."— CNBC's Erin Black contributed to this report.

title: Nvidia's role as AI financier faces first big test as neoclouds take market hit
description: Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA, presents new NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX Pod Full-Stack Modular AI Factory as he gives a keynote address at the Berlin GPU Tech
body: Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA, presents new NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX Pod Full-Stack Modular AI Factory as he gives a keynote address at the Berlin GPU Technology Conference (GTC) on October 21, 2026 in Berlin, Germany.Sean Gallup | Getty ImagesNvidia's emergence as financier for the global AI buildout is facing its first major stress test as credit markets tighten for key partners. After creating the chips that powered the early stages of the generative artificial intelligence era, Nvidia turned to using its financial prowess to fund AI model developers, data center companies and a host of so-called neoclouds. CEO Jensen Huang's strategy has been to not only build the most advanced technology but to provide customers with investment as well as help them take out loans so his systems can reach many more hands. That's meant taking full advantage of Nvidia's investment grade credit rating and providing backstop guarantees on mega-projects for OpenAI so that buildouts can get funded at lower interest rates. As of its last quarterly financial filing in July, Nvidia had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, in addition to its guarantee on up to $105 billion for chips, land and power at a proposed 10 gigawatt OpenAI data center in Ohio. The company signed as a tenant for $20 billion in future data center leases, which will later be assigned to third parties. For the vast majority of these deals, Nvidia won't have to pay up unless participants in the project default. "If the demand for compute doesn't meet these really super lofty expectations, we're going to have a problem," said David Trainer, founder and CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, in an interview. Nvidia declined to comment for this story. watch nowMarket conditions may soon test Nvidia's mettle. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, all cash-burning companies in Nvidia's portfolio, are down at least 30% this month. CoreWeave, the biggest of the group, has seen the spread on its credit default swaps soar past 11%, as investors are forced to pay up for insurance against default. Nvidia has backed other neoclouds that have run into challenges. The company is an investor in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus, which abruptly withdrew its IPO plans this month, as well as Nscale out of the U.K. and SoftBank-backed SB Energy. Both of those companies filed to go public in the U.S. in September but haven't provided updates on their plans in weeks.Nvidia wrapped up a third straight down week on Wall Street on Friday, with its stock now off 7.6% in October, on pace for its worst month since November of last year. Huang reiterated his confidence in the market this week, telling CNBC on Thursday that demand for neoclouds is "off the charts.""What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of the company's GTC conference in Berlin. "Because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital." Nvidia has taken equity stakes in dozens of companies, including big investments in OpenAI and Anthropic. Its portfolio is worth $99 billion as of the second quarter. Building the ecosystemInvestors told CNBC that a big question surrounding Nvidia is how the company can use its cash and $5 trillion market cap to get more chips into customers' hands, and how much risk it will assume in the process. Nvidia graphics processing units are critical for training and deploying AI models. Revenue in the latest fiscal year hit $216 billion, up roughly eightfold since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022. Before the AI boom, Nvidia sold graphics cards that could fit into a standard server rack or PC. Its newest systems are much larger and more expensive. Nvidia's flagship Vera Rubin product is a seven-foot rack containing 72 GPUs and weighing as much as a pickup truck. It costs more than $7 million, according to a Morgan Stanley estimate.While Nvidia still dominates the AI chip market, competition is emerging from the likes of Google, which rents out tensor processing units (TPUs) inside its massive cloud offering, and Advanced Micro Devices, which launched its first AI rack called Helios in July. watch nowCash is Nvidia's other great advantage. The company generated $70 billion in free cash flow in the first half of this year, while AMD totaled just over $4 billion and Google parent Alphabet went cash flow negative in the second quarter to fund its buildout.That's a big edge for Nvidia in building out its ecosystem. The company is now offering a full-service platform complete with software, services, integrated hardware and, for many customers, financing assistance.Nvidia's most recent quarterly financial filing in August outlined over $500 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments over the coming years, with a majority maturing through fiscal 2029. That same month, Huang announced a partnership with six large asset managers on a $500 billion financing push designed to treat compute infrastructure as an asset class. That agreement, which promised financial firms up to $125 billion in residual value guarantees on GPU financings, was in addition to the stakes Nvidia has taken as a limited partner in private equity funds. The company seeded $2 billion in Brookfield's inaugural AI Infrastructure Partners Fund, which aims to raise $10 billion in total capital, as well as other unconfirmed sums in KKR's Helix Digital Infrastructure (an $11 billion vehicle) and Valor Equity Partners' $5.4 billion dedicated compute fund."We used to build chips that we sell, and these are technology components that people buy and use," Huang told CNBC, in announcing the agreement in August. "But now, Nvidia's AI factory platform is really an investable asset."Huang has adopted a marketing mantra to reinforce the unique value of its equipment."We're the most rentable. We're fungible, and we're durable," he said on a podcast with investor Brad Gerstner published last week. 20 years of hardware in OhioWhile Nvidia waits for Wall Street firms to pull in investors to expand the GPU loan pool, the chipmaker is already actively fostering record-sized deals in the AI infrastructure space. Nvidia's biggest single guarantee is for OpenAI's forthcoming facility in Pike County, Ohio, which could be the largest data center in the world. That deal requires use of Nvidia hardware for at least 20 years. The shift from chips to capital carries significant risks should OpenAI run into trouble.If OpenAI misses payments or faces insolvency, Nvidia can take over the lease, find a new tenant, or ask the landlord, SB Energy, to sell the facility, guaranteeing to pay the difference for the latter two arrangements up to $105 billion if the release or sale falls below a minimum price. Nvidia could also pay SB Energy a lump sum. On the other side, if OpenAI posts its own collateral, or achieves a high enough credit rating, Nvidia's guarantee ends.At CoreWeave, Nvidia's investment includes equity and a commitment to buy up to $6.3 billion of its compute if it can't find another taker.Nvidia's backstops can take many forms, such as guaranteeing a minimum resale price or a minimum hourly offtake price for the chips in the event the lender has to recoup the assets. With Sharon AI and other neoclouds, Nvidia's deals have come with revenue-sharing agreements. "We believe these AI cloud partners have strong customer demand and robust sales pipelines but are constrained by the large-scale infrastructure that is required to meet that demand," Nvidia said in its quarterly filing.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreWeave and Nebius this monthHuang said this week that CoreWeave doesn't need Nvidia's backstop and that the neocloud's cost of capital is decreasing. CoreWeave has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans. Yields on its bonds maturing in 2031 and 2032 topped 15%. Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the market jitters reflect concerns about the stability of the business. CoreWeave and other neoclouds "will sign contracts into the future, and that all looks fine and dandy in their earnings reports, but is that contract going to be stable?" Stutland said. "Is it going to break at some point?" Nvidia says its financial support can help customers build the infrastructure needed to meet strong demand for its chips. More computing capacity could also help AI labs develop new models and services, creating further demand for Nvidia products."They'll do $700 billion in revenue next year," Deepwater Asset Management founder Gene Munster told CNBC last month. "That affords them the ability to finance some of their customers."Nvidia's credit backstops have mostly kicked in over the past six to 12 months. Its last annual filing, published in February, makes no mention of AI cloud agreements. Warren Hosseinion, co-founder of AI infrastructure startup Compute Labs, said Nvidia doesn't want to be in the position of insurer, "but they're willing to play that role while the market and the industry catches up.""They kind of control how things move," said Hosseinion, whose company tokenizes GPUs in order to open up pools of capital for neocloud operators. "They have to be very careful about how they release their technology at what pace, because a lot of that will dictate how the market moves around it."Not a 'complete panacea'Nvidia is actively looking for insurers to bear some of the risk associated with the potential loss in value of GPUs. "Insurers are not yet a complete panacea to this problem," said Tom Hoad, executive director of product innovation at global insurance group Howden. "But they are probably going to turn up and be helpful in the right situations, and therefore open up some commercial transactions." According to research from New Constructs, Nvidia's net present value of off-balance-sheet liabilities in fiscal 2026 totals over $153 billion, an increase of over $100 billion from last year.Such liabilities have been growing across the entire AI trade, mainly in the form of lease obligations. Ratings agencies like Moody's have been sounding the alarm. In 2026, guarantees are the fastest-growing type of off-balance-sheet financing arrangements, the agency said. Moody's doesn't count guarantees as debt when rating corporate buyers, but it's "something we're constantly monitoring," said David Gonzales, a vice president at the agency."These things are advanced structures that are unique, and so there is no blanket real approach you can take," he said. Gonzales said it's likely that chips will retain "values in excess of contractual residual value amounts" in the near future, which would mitigate risk in many of Nvidia's financing structures. Still, how much exposure investment grade AI players can handle is "the question we're evaluating at all times every day," Gonzales said."It's the center of all of our discussions right now," he said.— CNBC's Seema Mody contributed to this report.  WATCH: CNBC's full interview with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

schema.headline: Nvidia's role as AI financier faces first big test as neoclouds take market hit

title: AI's 'Black October': Critical PHP flaws set off global security scramble
description: Cybersecurity teams around the globe are rushing to patch PHP programming language flaws this week, in an artificial intelligence safety moment that's
body: Cybersecurity teams around the globe are rushing to patch PHP programming language flaws this week, in an artificial intelligence safety moment that's being described as "Black October."Nearly 70% of all websites use PHP, according to some estimates. "In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year," John Milinovich, senior director of product management at Figma, wrote in a post on X on Thursday. "Every sector from government to education to big tech and banks is being massively affected, and people are starting to freak out."Researchers at Google's Wiz and the AI firm Calif discovered major vulnerabilities in PHP in August by using advanced AI models from OpenAI and Google. But by Tuesday, the warnings had spread online, prompting governments and businesses around the globe to scramble to contain the fallout. Major AI companies have been warning about the technology's advancing cybersecurity capabilities since April, when Anthropic announced a limited rollout of its powerful model called Mythos. Concerns mounted in July, when OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached a company called Hugging Face. Experts believe the PHP security flaws serve as the latest example of what's to come.Jason Clinton, deputy chief information security officer at Anthropic, wrote in a post on X on Thursday that the cybersecurity landscape is likely to get "a lot worse" before it gets better."Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now," Clinton said. "Not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)"While many large companies have access to advanced models that they can use to harden their systems, serious bugs could be more challenging for small- and medium-sized businesses to address, Chris Krebs, former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, told CNBC on Friday. He encouraged smaller companies to "constantly" scan for vulnerabilities, deploy patches as fast as possible or take legacy systems offline."This is a significant week or two in cybersecurity," Krebs told CNBC's "Squawk Box." "As I mentioned, 3% of all critical vulnerabilities ever discovered have been found in the last month."Figma's Milinovich encouraged individuals to set up two-factor authentication for "everything," use a password manager, set up an identity protection app and move smart devices to their own network. He added that people should lean in and experiment with AI to understand how powerful the tools have become. "While I still firmly believe that AI will be a net positive for humanity, it's more clear to me than ever that the societal and individual risk is very real, and is playing out NOW," Milinovich said.Krebs added that company leaders and employees should check in on their security teams."Make sure they're doing okay," he said. "They've had a heck of a week."—CNBC's Isabel O’Brien contributed to this reportWATCH: Chris Krebs on AI discovering cyber vulnerabilities: It’ll get worse before it gets better

title: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted missiles and drones from Iran-backed Houthis
description: The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.AFP via Getty ImagesSaudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles headed for several cities,
body: The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.AFP via Getty ImagesSaudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles headed for several cities, including the capital Riyadh, fired by Iran-aligned Houthis on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.The ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Yemen-based Houthis, combined with remarks by President Donald Trump last week suggesting that the U.S. and Israel are planning fresh strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, drove oil prices to a six-month high Friday.The official Saudi Press Agency quoted the spokesperson of the Saudi-led Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen, Turki Al-Maliki, as saying two drones and a ballistic missile were "intercepted and destroyed" as they headed toward Riyadh. The agency quoted Al-Maliki as saying that 10 ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward the southern region of Saudi Arabia were also intercepted, as was a cruise missile headed for the city of Khamis Mushait.The Houthis said in a Telegram post that they "carried out seven qualitative military operations using a number of ballistic missiles and drones."The targets included Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and oil giant Saudi Aramco's facilities in Yanbu on Saudi Arabia's west coast as well as other airports and energy installations around the country, the Houthis said.Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid Airport, after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis said they attacked the airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, October 8, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video.Social Media/via ReutersKing Khalid International Airport said in a notice to travelers that it was resuming operations Sunday, using its Terminal 1 for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for overseas routes. The airport suspended operations on Oct. 10 following a strike that killed at least 13 people and injured around 300 others, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.Saudi Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Resumption of Iran attacks 'fairly soon'?While the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been exchanging strikes in recent weeks, concerns have been mounting among investors that the U.S. could soon resume its attacks on Iran.The U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia last week amid the Houthi attacks.Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. was not negotiating with Iran and something would happen "fairly soon." The president's cryptic remarks came as U.S. officials told The New York Times that the U.S. and Israel have plans for fresh strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.watch now"I think there's more and more fears of escalation in the Middle East," Amrita Sen, Founder and Director of Energy Aspects, told CNBC's Squawk Box Europe on Friday."We keep getting asked by clients: 'Is it going to be before the midterms? Is it after the midterms?' So it's not a question of 'if.' People are asking if it's a question of 'when.' Our view remains that it's more likely after the midterms than before." Rising tensions, worries about supply disruptions and concerns about possible fresh U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran helped push Brent crude to a six-month high Friday.Brent futures gained 3.1% to close at $116.72 a barrel, the highest international benchmark settlement since April 29. U.S. West Texas Intermediate added 3.8% to settle at $103.27 a barrel. Brent added 6.2% for the week, the third consecutive week of gains. WTI advanced 2.3% for the week.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBrent crude oil price, U.S. dollars per barrel, year to date

body: Around 800,000 people demonstrated across France, including 250,000 in Paris, according to the CGT. The march in Paris began at 2 pm from the Porte d'Italie and headed for the Porte de Vincennes after the route was changed by the Police Headquarters at the last minute. October 24, 2026. (Photo by Telmo Pinto/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesFrance's unrest is fueling investor concerns over the country's fiscal outlook, after borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2002 last week.Fund managers are assessing whether prolonged disruption could weaken growth, undermine confidence and make it harder for the government to deliver planned budget savings.Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in cities around France on Saturday. Largely peaceful rallies gave way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of last week's unrest.The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high.Rating agency Moody's on Friday kept its Aa3 credit rating on France, a level it still deems "high grade," but maintained its negative outlook on the nation."The negative outlook reflects the increased risk that the fragmentation of France's political landscape will continue to impair the functioning of the country's legislative institutions," Moody's said in its report.Moody's noted that it could return France's outlook to stable if its institutions can narrow its budget deficit.watch nowCan France's government pass its budget?France's government aims to reduce the budget deficit to 5% of GDP in 2027, from a projected 5.4% in 2026. The National Assembly is due to resume debating on the budget's tax measures, which are intended to generate savings, on Oct. 27 but opposition lawmakers are resisting the plans.Alain Durré, head of EMEA economic research at Natixis CIB, said the government was determined to prevent a sharp rise in borrowing costs.Durré said the government could try to stick to its fiscal targets by invoking Article 49.3 — which allows it to push a bill through the assembly without a final vote unless lawmakers can pass a no-confidence motion — or by using executive ordinances.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconFrance 10-Year OATs.That could help settle nerves and restore investor confidence, Durré added, noting that recent pressure on French sovereign debt has been driven primarily by tactical portfolio reallocations, with traditional buy-and-hold investors "still sitting on the sidelines."The yield on benchmark 10-year French government bonds, known as OATs, climbed 11 basis points Thursday to its highest level since 2002. That pushed the spread over 10-year German Bunds — the benchmark for euro zone debt — to its widest level since November 2011.Charlotte de Montpellier, senior economist for France and Switzerland at ING, said the unrest "adds another layer of uncertainty" to the budgetary and political concerns already weighing on French assets, and "reinforces the perception that any future government will find it difficult to deliver the reforms and savings required.""It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament," said Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at Ebury. "Even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed."What damage will the unrest do to France's growth outlook?Fresh demonstrations are planned for Oct. 24, and a union-backed national day of strikes and protests is set for Nov. 5, with anti-establishment Yellow Vest protestors among those calling for further rallies.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCAC 40.In a note on Oct. 20 after the violence of the previous weekend, de Montpellier said that, while the market can look past short-lived disruption, "a lasting loss of confidence can have a bigger impact.""These events further darken an economic outlook that was already unfavorable," she said. "We had expected French GDP growth of just 0.3% in 2026 and 0.6% in 2027. If the unrest continues, confidence deteriorates further or market tensions intensify, growth could be even weaker."The Yellow Vest movement may have reduced French GDP growth in the fourth quarter of 2018 by 0.1 percentage point, according to an INSEE estimate cited by de Montpellier. Industrial action during the spring 2023 pension protests reduced first-quarter GDP growth by around 0.1 percentage point, according to the Banque de France.In her Oct. 20 note, she said violence could keep households away from city centers and prompt tourists to postpone trips and businesses to delay investment. watch nowDurré said French consumer sentiment was already near historic lows before the latest protests, leaving little room for the country to absorb a fresh macroeconomic shock.He added the unrest raises "two key red flags" for markets."First, the risk that prolonged disruption drags on GDP growth. Second, fears that political pressure could derail government plans for critical spending cuts ... Either way, that would widen the deficit and blow past the government's 5% GDP target."Which French sectors are most exposed?France's CAC 40 has fallen 4.5% over the past month. ING identified retail, hospitality and tourism, and transport and logistics as the sectors most directly exposed to the turmoil.De Montpellier said shops and shopping centers face lower footfall, closures and lost sales; hotels, cafés, restaurants and travel services risk losing activity that customers are less likely to reschedule. Transport and logistics could also be hit if disruption persists, she added.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCarrefour.Carrefour shares plunged more than 14% Wednesday after the supermarket giant cut its profit outlook and reduced investment, citing the unrest — along with rising energy costs — as a drag on consumer sentiment. CEO Alexandre Bompard said the country faces an "unprecedented situation."More than 2,000 businesses had been directly affected by Tuesday, ING said, citing estimates from France's network of chambers of commerce.The impact could extend well beyond companies most directly exposed to the unrest, said Kevin Thozet, portfolio advisor and member of the investment committee at Carmignac.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconLVMH."For equities, this does not help banks, given the higher cost of equity, while prolonged uncertainty can slow loan growth and create credit problems," he told CNBC via email.France's prestigious luxury sector generates most of its sales abroad. LVMH has relatively limited direct exposure to the French market, with France accounting for just 8% of its 2025 revenue. But the demonstrations could weigh on tourism and therefore tax-free purchases, which account for around 20% of LVMH's revenue in France, Thozet said."A further six months of political vacuum is a very long time for markets, the economy and entrepreneurs," he added.

title: Marc Lore’s Wonder bets on Texas, automation and user-built restaurants as it mulls IPO
